Chapter 4 Random Variables and Probability Distributions In Statistics, we often have a dataset that we wish to explore and learn from. Typically, the dataset consists of a sample from our population of interest, and the observed values in the dataset are subject to randomness due to the nature of selecting the individuals to sample and then observing or measuring specific pieces of information as variables. Because of the randomness that typically affects the observed values in the dataset, we can think of our variables as being random variables. Thus, in order to learn from a dataset, we apply probability theory to characterize and work with random variables. 4.1 Random Variables Definition 4.1 A random variable (rv) is a rule that associates a number with each outcome of the sample space of a random experiment. We generally denote random variables by uppercase letters, such as \(X\), \(Y\), or \(Z\). From this point on in the book, we will use lowercase letters (\(x\), \(y\), \(z\)) to denote particular values of random variables. Example 4.1 The sample space for the random experiment of flipping a coin is \(\mathcal{S} = \{H, T\}\). We can define the rv \(X\) as equal to 0 if the result of the flip is tails and 1 if the result is heads. If we were to actually carry out a coin flip and observe, say, tails, we could then say that we observed \(x = 0\). Example 4.2 Define the rv \(Y\) as the number of calls to a help center in one week. The possible values of \(Y\) are \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\) (in theory, continuing to infinity). Example 4.3 Let \(Z\) be the percent purity of a chemical compound. \(Z\) can take any value in the interval \([0, 100]\). In the first two examples, the random variables were discrete, while the rv in the third example was continuous. Definition 4.2 A discrete random variable is an rv that can take a finite or at most countably infinite number of values. A continuous random variable is an rv that can take any value within an interval (possibly infinite) of the real number line. We will use the notation \(S_X\) to denote the possible values of a discrete rv \(X\). Almost always, \(S_X\) will be the first few counting numbers (say, 0, 1, 2, ...) 4.2 Probability Functions The probability distribution of an rv describes how much probability to assign to each value. There are a few functions that completely characterize a probability distribution. We will begin with the probability mass function for a discrete rv and then turn to the probability density function for a continuous rv. 4.2.1 Probability Mass Function (Discrete RVs) Definition 4.3 The probability mass function (pmf) of a discrete rv \(X\) is a function that returns the probabilities \(f(x) = P(X = x)\) for each value \(x\) in \(\mathcal{S}_X\). That is, the pmf defines the probability associated with each possible value of the discrete rv \(X\). Note that we must have that \(f(x) \geq 0\) for all \(x\) in \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(\sum_{x} f(x) = 1\). Example 4.4 In the coin flip example, suppose we purchase a special coin that is biased to land on heads with probability 0.6. With \(X\) again defined to be 0 in the case of tails and 1 in the case of heads, the pmf of \(X\) would have \(f(0) = 0.4\) and \(f(1) = 0.6\). To fully define the function, we can use the following: \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} 0.4 & \text{if } x = 0 \\ 0.6 & \text{if } x = 1 \\ 0 & \text{if } x \neq 0 \text{ or } 1 \end{cases} \] Example 4.5 Suppose we are studying the activity levels of a certain enzyme in a population of cells. The enzyme's activity can be categorized into five discrete levels. Let \(X\) be the rv that takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 if the activity level is very low, low, moderate, high, or very high, respectively. The pmf of \(X\) is \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} 0.10 & \text{if } x = 0 \\ 0.20 & \text{if } x = 1 \\ 0.30 & \text{if } x = 2 \\ 0.25 & \text{if } x = 3 \\ 0.15 & \text{if } x = 4 \\ 0 & \text{if } x \neq 0,1,2,3, \text{ or } 4 \end{cases} \] Figure 4.1 is a line graph visualization of the pmf. Figure 4.1: Enzyme activity example pmf 4.2.2 Probability Density Function (Continuous RVs) Definition 4.4 The probability density function (pdf) of a continuous rv \(X\) is a function \(f(x)\) such that, for any two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) with \(a \leq b\), \[ P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) dx \] That is, the probability that \(X\) takes a value in the interval \([a, b]\) equals the area under \(f(x)\) between \(a\) and \(b\) (an integral of \(f(x)\)). Note that \(f(x)\) is not equal to \(P(X = x)\). In fact, due to the continuous nature of the rv \(X\), \(P(X = x) = 0\). The pdf (as opposed to the pmf) can only be interpretted in terms of an integral over an interval. Example 4.6 Consider the time a student spends waiting for her bus to arrive. Suppose that the bus arrives at the stop every 10 minutes. If the student arrives at the bus stop at a randomly-specified time, without regard for the bus schedule, we might assume that the time spent (in minutes) waiting will follow the uniform distribution on the interval \([0, 10]\). The pdf of a rv \(X\) from the uniform distribution on the interval \([a, b]\) is \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{b-a} & \text{if } a \leq x \leq b \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \] In our example, we have \(a = 0\) and \(b = 10\), so our pdf would be \(f(x) = 1/10\) for all \(0 \leq x \leq 10\); reference Figure 4.2. Suppose we want to compute the probability that the student must wait between 1 and 3 minutes. The probability can be expressed as the following integral: \[ P(1 \leq X \leq 3) = \int_1^3 f(t) dt = \int_1^3 \frac{1}{10} dt = \frac{2}{10} \] The last equality reflects the fact that the uniform pdf is a rectangle, making our desired probability the area of a rectangle (height times width). Figure 4.2: Bus wait example pdf 4.3 Cumulative Distribution Function The pmf can be used to completely specify the probability distribution of a discrete rv. However, an alternative way to completely specify a probability distribution is in terms of cumulative probabilities of the form \(P(X \leq x)\). Definition 4.5 The cumulative distribution function (cdf) of a discrete rv \(X\) with pmf \(f(x)\) is a function that returns the (cumulative) probabilities \[ F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \sum_{t: t \leq x} f(t) \] for each value \(x\) in \(\mathcal{S}_X\). Example 4.7 Returning to the context of Example 4.5, we can obtain the cdf of \(X\) by computing \(F(x)\) for each \(x\) in \(\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\): \[\begin{align*} F(0) &= P(X \leq 0) = P(X = 0) = f(0) = 0.10 \\ F(1) &= P(X \leq 1) = P(X = 0 \text{ or } 1) = f(0) + f(1) = 0.30 \\ F(2) &= P(X \leq 2) = P(X = 0 \text{ or } 1 \text{ or } 2) = f(0) + f(1) + f(2) = 0.60 \\ F(3) &= P(X \leq 3) = P(X = 0 \text{ or } 1 \text{ or } 2 \text{ or } 3) = f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + f(3) = 0.85 \\ F(4) &= P(X \leq 4) = P(X = 0 \text{ or } 1 \text{ or } 2 \text{ or } 3 \text{ or } 4) = 1 \end{align*}\] The cdf would then be the step function shown in Figure 4.3. Figure 4.3: Enzyme activity example cdf There are only probability "jumps" or "steps" at the values \(x\) in \(\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\). For any other \(x\) value, \(F(x)\) is defined to be the cumulative probability for the nearest possible value of the rv \(X\) that is to the left of \(x\). For example, \(P(X \leq 1.4) = P(X \leq 1) = F(1) = 0.30\). We can now write the cdf as \[ F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x < 0 \\ 0.10 & \text{if } 0 \leq x < 1 \\ 0.30 & \text{if } 1 \leq x < 2 \\ 0.60 & \text{if } 2 \leq x < 3 \\ 0.85 & \text{if } 3 \leq x < 4 \\ 1 & \text{if } 4 \leq x \end{cases} \] In Example 4.7, we derived the cdf from the pmf. Note that we can also derive the pmf from the cdf. For example, \[\begin{align*} f(2) &= P(X = 2) \\ &= [f(0) + f(1) + f(2)] - [f(0) + f(1)] \\ &= P(X \leq 2) - P(X \leq 1) \\ &= F(2) - F(1) \end{align*}\] More generally, we can use the cdf to compute the probability that \(X\) falls within any interval. For example, again with reference to Example 4.7, \[\begin{align*} P(1 \leq X \leq 3) &= f(1) + f(2) + f(3) \\ &= [f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + f(3)] - f(0) \\ &= P(X \leq 3) - P(X \leq 0) \\ &= F(3) - F(0) \end{align*}\] Proposition 4.1 Let \(X\) be a discrete rv with possible values \(\mathcal{S}_X = \{x_1, x_2, \cdots\}\). The probability of an event of the form \([a \leq X \leq b]\) can be written in terms of the pmf as \[ P(a \leq X \leq b) = \sum_{a \leq x_i \leq b} f(x_i) \] and in terms of the cdf as \[ P(a \leq X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a-) \] where "\(a-\)" represents the largest possible \(X\) value that is strictly less than \(a\). In particular, if all of \(x_1, x_2, \ldots\) are integers and if \(a\) and \(b\) are integers, then \(P(a \leq X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a-1)\). Note the special case that when \(a = b\), \(P(X = a) = F(a) - F(a-1)\). Note that we can similarly use the cdf of a continuous rv to derive its pdf via the relationship \(f(x) = F'(x)\); that is, the pdf is obtained by differentiating the cdf. Definition 4.6 The cdf of a continuous rv \(X\) with pdf \(f(x)\) is a function that returns the cumulative probability \[ F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t) dt \] Example 4.8 Recall Example 4.6. The waiting time \(X\) (in minutes) follows a uniform distribution on the interval \([0, 10]\), i.e., \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,10)\). The cdf \(F(x)\) is obtained by integrating the pdf: \[ F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_0^x \frac{1}{10} dt = \frac{x}{10}, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 10 \] which leads to the full definition: \[ F(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & x < 0 \\ \frac{x}{10}, & 0 \leq x \leq 10 \\ 1, & x > 10 \end{cases} \] Figure 4.4 shows the graph of the cdf. Figure 4.4: Bus wait example cdf Suppose we want to compute the probability that a student must wait no more than 3 minutes for the bus. Using the CDF: \[ P(X \leq 3) = F(3) = \frac{3}{10} = 0.3 \] We can confirm the calculation in R using punif: punif(3, min = 0, max = 10) ## [1] 0.3 4.4 Discrete Distributions 4.4.1 Binomial Distribution A Bernoulli trial describes any random experiment that generates two outcomes. These are conventionally referred to as a "success" or a "failure". A Bernoulli random variable \(X\) takes the value 1 if the outcome is a success and the value 0 if it is a failure. Example 4.9 Flip a coin and designate heads as success and tails as failure. A cancer patient is either in remission (success) or not (failure). A smartphone is either defective (failure) or not (success). In each case, we could use the rv \(X\) to denote the outcome of an individual trial. Note that the choice of which outcome to call "success" is arbitrary. Let \(p\) be the probability of success for a Bernoulli rv (\(p = P(X = 1)\)). We can write the pmf simply: \[ f(x) = p^x(1-p)^{1-x} \] That is, \(f(x) = p\) when \(x = 1\) and \(f(x) = 1-p\) when \(x = 0\). Now consider running \(n\) Bernoulli trials, each with the same probability \(p\) of success, and with each trial being independent of all others, and suppose that we will count up the number of successes out of the \(n\) trials. This is defined as a binomial experiment, and the variable \(X\) that records the number of successes out of the \(n\) trials is called a binomial random variable. Letting \(X_i\) be the Bernoulli rv associated with the \(i\)th Bernoulli trial, we can write the binomial rv \(Y\) as \[ Y = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \] Thus, \(Y\) can take any of the integer values between 0 (all \(X_i = 0\)) and \(n\) (all \(X_i = 1\)), inclusive. We will write \(Y \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)\) to indicate that \(Y\) is a binomial rv and its probability distribution has parameters \(n\) and \(p\). We will now derive the binomial pmf. To begin, consider the case where \(n = 5\) (e.g., we flip a coin 5 times and count the number of heads) and suppose that we wish to compute the probability of the specific outcome \(FFFSS\) (that is, the first 3 flips are tails and the last 2 flips are heads). Since the trials are independent, the probability of this outcome is the product of the individual Bernoulli probabilities: \[\begin{align*} P(FFFSS) &= P(F) \cdot P(F) \cdot P(F) \cdot P(S) \cdot P(S) \\ &= (1-p) \cdot (1-p) \cdot (1-p) \cdot p \cdot p \\ &= p^2 (1-p)^3. \end{align*}\] While it is true that \(Y = 2\) in the above scenario, it is not true that \(P(Y=2)\) equals \(P(FFFSS)\). The reason for this is that there are multiple outcomes to the \(n = 5\) Bernoulli trials for which \(Y\) would equal 2 (\(FFFSS\) is just one of the possible outcomes). In fact, using our counting tools from Chapter 3, we know that there are \(\binom{5}{2} = 10\) ways to choose 2 successes out of 5 trials: \[ FFFSS, FFSFS, FFSSF, FSFFS, FSFSF, FSSFF, SFFFS, SFFSF, SFSFF, SSFFF \] To compute \(P(Y=2)\), we need to add up the probabilities of each outcome for which \(Y=2\). Since the probability is \(p^2(1-p)^3\) for each of these outcomes, we have \(P(Y=2) = 10p^2(1-p)^3\). Theorem 4.1 If \(Y \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)\), the pmf of \(Y\) is \[ P(Y=y) = \binom{n}{y} p^y (1-p)^{n-y}, \hspace{1cm} y=0, 1, \ldots, n \] Note that, while in Examples 4.4 and 4.5 we explicitly specified that \(f(x) = 0\) when \(x\) is not in \(\mathcal{S}_X\), here (and in the rest of the book), this is implied but not stated. To be clear, \(P(Y = y) = 0\) for any \(y\) not in \(\left\{ 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n \right\}\). Example 4.10 A factory produces light bulbs, and 10% of them are defective. You randomly select 10 light bulbs. What is the probability that exactly 2 of them are defective? What is the probability that at least 2 of them are defective? Solution: Let \(Y\) be the number of defective light bulbs out of the \(10\) that were sampled. We have that \(Y \sim \text{Bin}(n=10,p=0.10)\). \(P(Y=2) = \binom{10}{2} 0.10^2 0.90^8 = 0.1937102\) \[\begin{align*} P(Y \geq 2) &= 1 - P(Y \leq 1) \\ &= 1 - \binom{10}{0} 0.10^0 0.90^{10} - \binom{10}{1} 0.10^1 0.90^9 \\ &= 0.2639011 \end{align*}\] Figure 4.5 is a line graph visualization of the pmf. Figure 4.5: Light bulb example pmf There are four binomial-specific functions in R: dbinom: Evaluate the pmf pbinom: Evaluate the cdf qbinom: Return a percentile rbinom: Generate random realizations For example, the probabilities in Example 4.10 can be computed as follows: dbinom(2, 10, 0.10) ## [1] 0.1937102 1 - pbinom(1, 10, 0.10) ## [1] 0.2639011 Example 4.11 In a multiple-choice exam with 20 questions, each question has 4 answer choices. Suppose a student guesses on every question. What is the probability that they get at least 15 questions correct? Solution: Let \(Y\) be the number of correct answers based on guessing, so that \(Y \sim \text{Bin}(n=20, p=0.25)\). We can write the desired probability as \(P(Y \geq 15) = 1 - P(Y \leq 14)\) and use pbinom: 1 - pbinom(14, 20, 0.25) ## [1] 3.813027e-06 4.4.2 Distributions Related to the Bernoulli There are other random experiment scenarios that involve independent Bernoulli trials and are therefore related to the binomial experiment. The binomial distribution can be thought of as involving sampling from an infinite population of "successes" (\(S\text{'s}\)) and "failures" (\(F\text{'s}\)). The hypergeometric distribution, on the other hand, applies when we sample \(S\text{'s}\) and \(F\text{'s}\) (without replacement) from a finite population. The binomial distribution involves a fixed number of Bernoulli trials, based on which we count the number of \(S\)'s. The negative binomial distribution, by contrast, applies when we conduct trials until a specified number \(r\) of \(S\text{'s}\) is observed; the geometric distribution applies in the special case when \(r = 1\) (i.e., we conduct trials until the first \(S\)). Finally, the Poisson distribution is typically applied to counts of events that occur in a particular interval of time or space. While it does not correspond to any simple experiment, like a Bernoulli trial, there is a limiting relationship between the Poisson distribution and binomial distribution. 4.4.2.1 Geometric Distribution Before turning to the hypergeometric, let's cover the geometric distribution. As opposed to the Binomial example of counting the number of successes out of \(n\) trials, let's consider another question of interest: how many failures would we have to observe before we see the first success (that is, see an \(X_i = 1\)). Intuitively, as \(p\) gets closer to 1, we should have to see fewer trials as \(p = P(X_i = 1)\). The probability we see a success on the first trial is \(p\). Hence, we would say the for a rv \(X \sim geom(p)\), \(P(X = 0) = p\) as we would have observed no failures. However, suppose we see 1 failure before our first success, then \(P(X = 1) = P(FS) = (1-p)*p\). Therefore, in general, \[ P(X = x) = f(x) = (1-p)^xp \] for \(x = 0, 1, \ldots\). Note that it could theoretically take infinitely long, but the probability goes to zero very fast. How fast, you ask? Geometrically, of course! Example 4.12 We are monitoring a production run of circuit boards. We need to run the machine until it produces a defective circuit board so we can calibrate our new machine. At the speed we are running, the probability of producing a defective circuit board is 0.0001 and produces 1,000 circuit boards an hour. We want to know what is the probability that we will get a defective circuit board in less than 1.5 hours. Solution: We would produce 1,500 circuit boards in 1.5 hours. Hence, we want to know if we will get the first defective circuit board on the first, second, third, ..., 1,500th try. This corresponds to: \[ P(X \leq 1499) = f(0) + f(1) + \cdots + f(1499) = F(1499). \] We can find this via R with the pgeom function, which evaluates the cdf of the geometric(.0001) distribution: pgeom(1499,.0001) ## [1] 0.1392985 4.4.2.2 Hypergeometric Distribution The canonical example that is used to illustrate the hypergeometric distribution is that of counting the number of red balls in a simple random sample of \(n\) balls (sampled without replacement) selected from an urn that contains \(N\) balls, \(M\) of which are red and \(N-M\) of which are black; reference Section 2.3.1 for a reminder of what a simple random sample is. Crucially, the population in the context of a hypergeometric experiment is finite. Proposition 4.2 Let \(X\) be the number of \(S\)'s in a simple random sample of size \(n\) drawn from a population consisting of \(M\) \(S\)'s and \((N-M)\) \(F\)'s; that is, \[ X \sim \text{Hypergeometric}(n, M, N) \] The pmf of \(X\) is \[ P(X = x) = \frac{\binom{M}{x} \binom{N-M}{n-x}}{\binom{N}{n}} \] for any integer \(x\) such that \(\text{max}(0, n - N + M) \leq x \leq \text{min}(n, M)\). Example 4.12 Consider the canonical example: An urn contains \(N = 15\) balls, \(M = 5\) of which are red and \(N - M = 10\) of which are black. We randomly select \(n = 7\) balls (without replacement) and count the number \(X\) of red balls in our sample. What is \(P(X = 5)\)? What is \(P(X \leq 1)\)? Solution: \[ P(X = 5) = \frac{\binom{5}{5} \binom{10}{2}}{\binom{15}{7}} = 0.006993007 \] \[ P(X \leq 1) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) = \frac{\binom{5}{0} \binom{10}{7}}{\binom{15}{7}} + \frac{\binom{5}{1} \binom{10}{6}}{\binom{15}{7}} = 0.1818182 \] As with the binomial distribution, there are R functions dhyper, phyper, qhyper, and rhyper for the pmf, cdf, percentiles, and random realizations, respectively, with the hypergeometric distribution. For example, we can match the calculations in Example 4.12 as follows: dhyper(5, 5, 10, 7) ## [1] 0.006993007 phyper(1, 5, 10, 7) ## [1] 0.1818182 Example 4.13 In Example 4.10, the context was defective lightbulbs. We implicitly assumed that there were an infinite number of lightbulbs in the population. Suppose, however, that we limit our attention to a batch of \(N = 80\) lightbulbs, assuming again that 10% (\(M = 8\)) of them are defective. We again take a sample of size \(n = 10\). Let \(X\) be the number of defective lightbulbs in our sample, so \(X \sim \text{hypergeometric}(10, 8, 80)\). What is \(P(X = 2)\)? What is \(P(X \geq 2)\)? Solution: \[ P(X = 2) = \frac{\binom{8}{2} \binom{72}{8}}{\binom{80}{10}} = 0.2035433 \] \[\begin{align*} P(X \geq 2) &= 1 - P(X \leq 1) \\ &= 1 - \frac{\binom{8}{0} \binom{72}{10}}{\binom{80}{10}} - \frac{\binom{8}{1} \binom{72}{9}}{\binom{80}{10}} \\ &= 0.2607824 \end{align*}\] Both Examples 4.10 and 4.13 involved defective lightbulbs. The population was assumed to be infinite in Example 4.10 but treated as finite in Example 4.13. In both examples, we computed the same probabilities. When the population was treated as infinite, we had \(P(X = 2) \approx 0.19\) and \(P(X \geq 2) \approx 0.26\). In the finite population case, we had \(P(X = 2) \approx 0.20\) and \(P(X \geq 2) \approx 0.26\), reflecting only a minor difference. Probability differences would become more pronounced if the population size were made smaller. For example, changing \(N\) from 80 to 20 results in \(P(X = 2) \approx 0.08\) and \(P(X \geq 2) \approx 0.99\). As a rule of thumb, the binomial distribution gives approximately correct probabilities with a finite population as long as \(n/N\) is "small" (\(0.05\) is a common threshold) and \(M/N\) is not "too close" to 0 or 1 (\(0.1 \leq M/N \leq 0.9\), say). 4.4.2.3 Negative Binomial Distribution Proposition 4.3 Let \(X\) be the number of trials required to achieve \(r\) successes in a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials, where each trial has the same probability \(p\) of success. Then, \[ X \sim \text{NegBin}(r, p) \] The pmf of \(X\) is given by \[ P(X = x) = \binom{x-1}{r-1} p^r (1-p)^{x-r}, \hspace{1cm} x = r, r+1, r+2, \ldots \] where \(x\) is the total number of trials, and \(r\) is the number of required successes. Example 4.14 In the context of the defective lightbulb example, suppose we are interested in how many bulbs will need to be inspected before we find the third defective bulb. Letting \(X\) be the number of lightbulbs that need to be inspected before finding the third defective lightbulb. Then, \(X \sim \text{NegBin}(r=3, p=0.10)\). To find the probability that the third defective bulb is discovered on the seventh test, we use the pmf of the negative binomial distribution: \[\begin{align*} P(X = 7) &= \binom{7-1}{3-1} 0.10^3 0.90^{7-3} \\ &= 15 (0.10^3)(0.90^4) = 0.0098415 \end{align*}\] The dnbinom, pnbinom, qnbinom, and rnbinom functions in R can be used for negative binomial values, cumulative probabilities, quantiles, and random numbers. Note that there are multiple parameterizations for the negative binomial distribution, so you should always verify that you know how exactly the software you are using is set up. In R, for example, to match the probability calculation in Example 4.14, the first argument to dnbinom must be the number of non-defective bulbs that are found before the third defective bulb: dnbinom(7-3, 3, 0.10) ## [1] 0.0098415 Similarly, if we wish to randomly generate negative binomial observations in R according to our parameterization, we need to add \(r\) to the result of calling rnbinom. For example, here is a random sample of 5 observations from the \(\text{NegBin}(r=3, p=0.10)\) distribution: 3 + rnbinom(5, 3, 0.10) ## [1] 16 13 30 28 29 4.4.2.4 Poisson Distribution Definition 4.7 Let \(X\) be a rv that can take the values \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\). Then, \[ X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) \] means that the pmf of \(X\) is \[ P(X = x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^x}{x!} \] where \(\lambda > 0\). The letter \(e\) in the pmf expression is the base of the natural logarithm, equal to approximately 2.71828. To show that the claimed pmf sums to one, we can use the fact that \(e^{\lambda} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left( \lambda^k / k! \right)\). In R, see the functions dpois, ppois, qpois, and rpois. Example 4.15 Suppose the number of emails received by a company's customer support service follows a Poisson distribution with rate \(\lambda = 25\). What is the probability of receiving exactly 20 support emails in a day? What is the probability of receiving at least 40 support emails in a day? Solution: Let \(X\) be the number of support emails received in a day; \(X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 25)\). \(P(X = 20) = e^{-25} \frac{25^{20}}{20!} = 0.05191747\). We can confirm this via dpois(20, 25). \(P(X \geq 40) = 1 - P(X \leq 39)\). We can compute this via 1-ppois(39, 25), which returns \(0.003443569\). 4.4.2.4.1 Poisson as a Binomial Limit While the Poisson distribution was not defined in terms of Bernoulli trials, there is a limiting relationship between the Poisson and binomial distributions. Proposition 4.4 Let \(b(x; n, p)\) be the pmf for a binomial rv and \(f(x; \lambda)\) be the pmf for a Poisson rv. If we let \(n \rightarrow \infty\) and \(p \rightarrow 0\) in such a way that \(np\) approaches a value \(\lambda > 0\), then \(b(x; n, p) \rightarrow f(x; \lambda)\). Thus, in the context of a binomial experiment, if \(n\) is large and \(p\) is small, probabilities can be approximated by the Poisson distribution with \(\lambda = np\). A rule of thumb for applying this approximation is \(n \geq 100\) and \(np < 10\). Figure 4.6 illustrates the approximation, using the \(\text{Bin}(n=100, p=0.05)\) and \(\text{Poisson}(5)\) distributions. Figure 4.6: Illustration of Poisson approximation to binomial 4.5 Continuous Distributions 4.5.1 Exponential Distribution The exponential distribution is commonly used to model waiting times until an event occurs. Examples include the time until a lightbulb burns out, the time until a customer arrives at a service counter, or the time between earthquakes in a given region. Proposition 4.5 A continuous rv \(X\) follows the exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\lambda > 0\), written \[ X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda) \] if its probability density function (pdf) is given by \[ f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \hspace{1cm} x > 0 \] where \(\lambda\) is the rate of occurrence of events. Figure 4.7: Example exponential distribution pdfs Figure 4.7 shows a few examples of exponential pdfs with different values of \(\lambda\). Example 4.16 Suppose that customers arrive at a coffee shop at an average rate of 5 per hour. The time \(X\) (in hours) until the next customer arrives can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate \(\lambda = 5\); i.e., \(X \sim \text{Exp}(5)\). What is the probability that the next customer arrives within 10 minutes? Solution: We seek \(P(X \leq 10/60)\). This is a left-tail probability, given by the cumulative distribution function (cdf): \[ P(X \leq x) = \int_0^x \lambda e^{-\lambda t}dt = 1 - e^{-\lambda x} \] Substituting \(\lambda = 5\) and \(x = 10/60\): \[ P(X \leq 10/60) = 1 - e^{-5(10/60)} = 1 - e^{-5/6} \] In R, we can compute this probability using the pexp function: pexp(10/60, rate = 5) ## [1] 0.5654018 4.5.1.1 Memoryless Property A notable property of the exponential distribution is that it is memoryless. This means that the probability of waiting an additional time \(t\) does not depend on how long one has already waited: \[ P(X > s+t | X > s) = P(X > t) \] for all \(s, t > 0\). This property is unique to the exponential distribution among all continuous distributions. 4.5.1.2 Poisson-Exponential Connection The exponential and Poisson distributions are closely related. Specifically, the exponential distribution models the waiting time between successive arrivals in a Poisson process. Proposition 4.6 If events occur according to a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) per unit time, then the waiting time \(X\) between successive events follows an exponential distribution: \(X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)\). Proof. Consider the Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda\) for the number of events occurring in an interval of length \(t\) (call this number \(N(t)\)). The probability that no event occurs up to time \(t\) is equivalent to the probability that the waiting time exceeds \(t\): \[ P(X > t) = P(N(t) = 0) = e^{-\lambda t} \] The expression \(P(X > t)\) is called the survival function and equals one minus the cdf: \(P(X > t) = 1 - F(t) = 1 - P(X \leq t)\). As noted at the end of Section 4.3, we can obtain a pdf by differentiating the cdf. Here, differentiating both sides with respect to \(t\) yields the exponential pdf: \[ f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x > 0 \] Example 4.17 A customer service call center receives calls at an average rate of 12 per hour. The number of calls in an hour follows a Poisson distribution with \(\lambda = 12\). What is the probability that the next call will arrive within 5 minutes? What is the probability that no calls will arrive in a 15-minute interval? Solution: (a) The waiting time \(X\) follows an exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda = 12\). We compute: \[ P(X \leq 5/60) = 1 - e^{-12(5/60)} \] pexp(5/60, rate = 12) ## [1] 0.6321206 The probability that no calls arrive in a 15-minute interval is the probability that the waiting time exceeds 15 minutes: \[ P(X > 15/60) = e^{-12(15/60)} \] 1 - pexp(15/60, rate = 12) ## [1] 0.04978707 According to the Poisson-exponential connection, we can also express the above probability for waiting time in terms of a Poisson rv. In particular, defining \(Y \sim \text{Poisson(3)}\) (with the rate parameter value of 3 reflecting that, on average, 3 events occur every 15 minutes), we have that \[ P(X > 15/60) = P(Y = 0) = e^{-3} \] We can verify the calculation using dpois: dpois(0, lambda = 3) ## [1] 0.04978707 4.5.2 Gamma Distribution To define the gamma distribution, we first define the gamma function. Definition 4.8 The Gamma function, denoted as \(\Gamma(\alpha)\), is a generalization of the factorial function to positive real numbers and is defined as: \[ \Gamma(\alpha) = \int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1} e^{-x} dx, \quad \alpha > 0. \] Some important properties of the Gamma function are: \(\Gamma(\alpha) = (\alpha - 1) \Gamma(\alpha - 1)\) For a positive integer \(n\), \(\Gamma(n) = (n - 1)!\) \(\Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}\) Definition 4.9 A continuous rv \(X\) follows a gamma distribution with shape parameter \(\alpha > 0\) and rate parameter \(\lambda > 0\) if its pdf is: \[ f(x; \alpha, \lambda) = \frac{\lambda^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)} x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x > 0. \] We denote this as \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \lambda)\). Figure 4.8: Example gamma distribution pdfs Figure 4.8 shows a few examples of gamma pdfs with different values of \(\alpha\), keeping \(\lambda = 1\) for simplicity. The parameter \(\lambda\) serves as a scaling factor: increasing \(\lambda\) compresses the distribution, shifting the density toward smaller values of \(x\), while decreasing \(\lambda\) stretches the distribution, shifting the density toward larger values. Example 4.18 Suppose the time (in minutes) that a customer spends waiting in line at a bank follows a gamma distribution with \(\alpha = 3\) and \(\lambda = 0.5\). What is the probability that a customer waits between 4 and 7 minutes? Solution: Let \(X\) denote the waiting time. We have \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(3, 0.5)\). The probability we seek is: \[ P(4 \leq X \leq 7) = P(X \leq 7) - P(X \leq 4). \] Using R: pgamma(7, shape = 3, rate = 0.5) - pgamma(4, shape = 3, rate = 0.5) ## [1] 0.3558292 Note: In Example 4.18, we wrote \(P(4 \leq X \leq 7)\) as the difference of cumulative probabilities \(P(X \leq 7) - P(X \leq 4)\). Strictly speaking, we might instead write the difference as \(P(X \leq 7) - P(X < 4)\). However, as was pointed out in Section 4.2.2, with a continuous rv, the probability of any one possible realized value equals 0; i.e., for a continuous rv, \(P(X \leq x) = P(X < x)\). 4.5.3 Chi-Squared Distribution The Chi-Squared distribution arises frequently in statistical applications, particularly in hypothesis testing and variance estimation. Definition 4.10 A random variable \(X\) follows a Chi-Squared Distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom (denoted \(X \sim \chi^2_{\nu}\)) if its pdf is given by \[ f(x; \nu) = \frac{1}{2^{\nu/2} \Gamma(\nu/2)} x^{(\nu/2)-1} e^{-x/2}, \quad x > 0 \] where \(\nu > 0\) is the degrees of freedom, and \(\Gamma(\cdot)\) is the gamma function. Figure 4.9: Example chi-squared distribution pdfs Example 4.19 A company monitors the temperature of a critical machine component every hour. Based on historical data, the sum of squared deviations of these temperature readings from a target value follows a Chi-Squared distribution with \(\nu = 8\) degrees of freedom. If the sum of squared deviations exceeds 15, an alarm is triggered. What is the probability that the alarm is triggered in any given hour? Solution: We need to compute \(P(X > 15)\) for \(X \sim \chi^2(8)\): \[ P(X > 15) = 1 - P(X \leq 15) \] Using pchisq in R: 1 - pchisq(15, df = 8) ## [1] 0.05914546

Chapter 5 Expected Value Recall our discussion in Chapter 2 of populations, parameters, samples, and sample statistics. A parameter is a numeric characteristic of the population of interest. Often, parameters can be defined in terms of expected values. Expected value can be thought of as a weighted average. If we write down the usual, unweighted average: \[ \overline{X} =  rac{1}{n} \sum_{ i=1}^n X_i =  rac{1}{n}X_1 + \cdots  rac{1}{n}X_n \] we can see that we are equally weighting each term in the sum by \(1/n\). This can be generalized to a weighted average by making these weights not equal to each other. A prominent example in your academic lives is your total grade in a class Example 5.1 Suppose a class rubric weights the total scores for a class like: 10% quizzes, 40% homework, 25% for a midterm, and 25% for final. If a student has scores in each of these categories of 85%, 87%, 88%, and 95%, then this student's total score in the class would be \[ 86*.1 + 88*.4 + 90*.25 + 95*.25 = 90.05 \] Compare this to an equally weight rubric where each category has the same 25% weight: \[ 86*.25 + 88*.25 + 90*.25 + 95*.25 = 89.75 \] In either case, the average is found via the general procedure of: "sum" of the "values" times the "weights". This will be the same idea for expected value in what follows. In Section 2.5, we introduced the mean as a way of characterizing a "typical value" for a variable. We will formalize this now. As the mathematical device is different for discrete and continuous variables, we will treat them separately. The overall idea is the same. 5.1 Expected Value for Discrete Variables Definition 5.1 Let \(X\) be a discrete rv with set of possible values \(\mathcal{S}_X\) and pmf \(f(x)\). The expected value or population mean of \(X\) is \[ E[X] = \mu_X = \sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} x \cdot f(x) \] Note that this, like the weighted average, has the form "sum" of "values" times the "weights". The term \(\sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X}\) deserves some comment. The just represents the idea that in different problems, the valid values for \(X\) might be different. Commonly, \(X\) will take on just the first few integers, such as \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3\) and hence \(\mathcal{S}_X = \{0,1,2,3\}\) and \(\sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} = \sum_{ x = 0}^3\) Example 5.2 In the context of Example 4.5, where a certain enzyme's activity can be categorized into five discrete levels: \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\), then \(\mathcal{S}_X = {0,1,2,3,4}\). We can find the expected value of \(X\): \[ egin{align*} E[X] = \mu_X &= 0 \cdot f(0) + 1 \cdot f(1) + 2 \cdot f(2) + 3 \cdot f(3) + 4 \cdot f(4) \ &= (0)(0.10) + (1)(0.20) + (2)(0.30) + (3)(0.25) + (4)(0.15) \ &= 2.15 \end{align*}\] Note that 2.15 is not one of the possible values of \(X\). The expected value in Example 5.2 can be easily computed in R: x <- 0:4 f_x <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.25, 0.15) sum(x * f_x) ## [1] 2.15 There is actually nothing special about computing the expected value of \(X\) itself. In fact, we can, and often will, compute expected values of functions of \(X\), \(h(X\)): Definition 5.2 Let \(X\) be a discrete rv with set of possible values \(\mathcal{S}_X\) and pmf \(f(x)\). The expected value of the discrete random variable \(h(X)\) is \[ E[h(X)] = \sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} h(x) f(x) \] Again, this should be thought of as a weighted average. Except, now the values are \(h(x)\) instead of just \(x\). Here is an example: Example 5.3 A grocery store purchases five crates of fresh produce at $30 each and will sell them for $60 each. The store has an agreement that any unused crates can be returned at the end of a week for $10 each. Let \(X\) be the number of crates sold during the week, and suppose that \(f(0) = 0.10, f(1) = 0.15, f(2) = 0.25, f(3) = 0.30, f(4) = 0.15\), and \(f(5) = 0.05\). Net revenue, denoted as \(h(X)\), can be calculated as \[ h(X) = 60X + 10(5 - X) - 150 = 50X - 100 \] Expected net revenue is \[ egin{align*} E[h(X)] &= h(0) \cdot f(0) + h(1) \cdot f(1) + h(2) \cdot f(2) + h(3) \cdot f(3) + h(4) \cdot f(4) + h(5) \cdot f(5) \ &= (-100)(0.10) + (-50)(0.15) + (0)(0.25) + (50)(0.30) + (100)(0.15) + (150)(0.05) \ &= \$20 \end{align*}\] Notice in Example 5.3 that we did not have to derive the pmf of \(h(X)\). We computed \(E[h(X)]\) in terms of the pmf of \(X\). This is because while the values changed, the weights (that is, the pmf) did not. The following R code can be used: x <- 0:5 f_x <- c(0.10, 0.15, 0.25, 0.30, 0.15, 0.05) h <- function(x) { 50 * x - 100 } h_x <- h(x) sum(h_x * f_x) ## [1] 20 5.2 Expected Value for Continuous Variables For a continuous rv, instead of \(E[X]\) being a weighted average (possible values of \(X\) weighted by the pmf), \(E[X]\) is an integral. Definition 5.3 Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with pdf \(f(x)\). The expected value or population mean of \(X\) is defined as \[ E[X] = \mu_X = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x)\, dx \] Recall (e.g., reference Example 4.6) the definition of the uniform distribution for a continuous rv. Example 5.4 Suppose our company manufactures biodegradable paper straws, and we are concerned about consumer complaints that the straws fall apart before they finish their drink. Let \(X\) be the length of time (in minutes) that a straw remains intact while being used. Suppose this time is uniformly distributed between 10 and 20 minutes: \[ X \sim 	ext{Uniform}(10, 20) \] Then the probability density function (pdf) of \(X\) is: \[ f(x) =  egin{cases}  rac{1}{10}, & 10 \leq x \leq 20 \\ 0, & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} \] The expected value of \(X\) is: \[ E[X] = \int_{10}^{20} x \cdot  rac{1}{10} \, dx =  rac{1}{10} \int_{10}^{20} x \, dx =  rac{1}{10} \left[  rac{x^2}{2} ight]_{10}^{20} =  rac{1}{10} \left(  rac{400}{2} -  rac{100}{2} ight) = 15 \] Thus, on average, a paper straw from our production line lasts 15 minutes before deteriorating. Similarly to discrete random variables, we will want to compute the expected value of functions of continuous random variables. Fortunately, this works in way you would 'expect': Definition 5.4 Let \(X\) be a continuous rv with pdf \(f(x)\). The expected value of the random variable \(h(X)\) is \[ E[h(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x) f(x)\, dx \] 5.3 Expected Value for Linear Functions When the function \(h(X)\) is a particularly simple function, we can simplify our results: Proposition 5.1 For the linear function \(h(X) = aX + b\), \[ E[h(X)] = E[aX + b] = a \cdot E[X] + b \] In words, this means that for linear functions, the "expected value of the function" is the "function of the expected value". Proof. For discrete random variables: \[ egin{align*} E[aX + b] &= \sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} (ax + b) f(x) = a \sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} x \cdot f(x) + b\sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} f(x) \ &= aE[X] + b \end{align*}\] Note that the proof follows for continuous random variables almost identically due to integration being a linear operation just like summation. Example 5.5 In the context of Example 5.3, we can compute the expected value of \(X\): \[ E[X] = \sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} x \cdot f(x) = 2.4 \] Therefore: \[ E[h(X)] = E[50X - 100] = 50E[X] - 100 = 50*2.4 - 100 = \$20 \] Likewise, we can apply Proposition 5.1 to continuous random variables. Example 5.6 Suppose our company issues a 10¢ refund to customers if their paper straw lasts less than 14 minutes before breaking down. Let \(Y = h(X)\) denote the cost to the company for a single straw that lasts \(X\) minutes. Then the cost function is: \[ h(x) =  egin{cases} 10, & x < 14 \\ 0, & x \geq 14 \end{cases} \] To compute the expected cost per straw, we calculate \(E[h(X)]\): \[ E[h(X)] = \int_{10}^{20} h(x) f(x)\, dx \] Since \(f(x) =  rac{1}{10}\) on the interval \([10, 20]\) and \(h(x) = 10\) only when \(x < 14\): \[ E[h(X)] = \int_{10}^{14} 10 \cdot  rac{1}{10} \, dx + \int_{14}^{20} 0 \cdot  rac{1}{10} \, dx = \int_{10}^{14} 1 \, dx = 14 - 10 = 4 \] Thus, the expected cost per straw is 4¢. 5.4 Variance and Standard Deviation In Section 2.5, we also introduced the sample variance and sample standard deviation as ways of characterizing the "spread" of a variable. When referencing a random variable we can compute the population variance and the population standard deviation. The idea is we want to quantify "how far" "on average" we "expect" values of the random variable to be from its "mean". Let's make this precise: Definition 5.5 Let \(X\) be a rv with population mean \(\mu_X\). The variance of \(X\), denoted by \(	ext{Var}[X]\) or \(\sigma^2_X\), is \[ \sigma_X^2 = 	ext{Var}[X] = E \left[ (X - \mu_X)^2 ight] =  egin{cases} \sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} (x - \mu_X)^2 f(x) & 	extrm{ if $X$ is discrete} \ \int_{-\infty}^\infty (x - \mu_X)^2 f(x) \, dx & 	extrm{ if $X$ is continuous} \end{cases} \] The standard deviation of \(X\) is \[ \sigma_X = +\sqrt{\sigma^2_X} \] According to its definition, the variance of \(X\) is the mean of the quantity \((X - \mu)^2\). That is, the variance represents a "typical value" of the squared difference between \(X\) and its mean. If the probability distribution is closely packed around \(\mu\), this squared difference will tend to be small, which means \(\sigma^2_X\) will be small. Conversely, if \(X\) is frequently far from \(\mu\), \(\sigma^2_X\) will be large. Example 5.7 Following Example 5.2 where we computed \(\mu_X = 2.15\), we can find the variance as well: \[ egin{align*} 	ext{Var}[X] = \sigma^2_X &= \sum_{ \mathcal{S}_X} (x - 2.15)^2 \cdot f(x) \ &= (0 - 2.15)^2(0.10) + (1 - 2.15)^2(0.20) + \cdots + (4 - 2.15)^2(0.15) \ &= 1.4275 \end{align*}\] The standard deviation is \(\sigma_X = \sqrt{1.4275} = 1.19478\). Here is the calculation in R: x <- 0:4 f_x <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.25, 0.15) mu <- sum(x * f_x) sum((x - mu) ^ 2 * f_x) ## [1] 1.4275 The following "shortcut" formula will almost always be used as it is easier to use: Proposition 5.2 \[ 	ext{Var}[X] = \sigma^2_X = E \left[ X^2 ight] - \left( E[X] ight)^2 \] Note that the order of the brackets and the square are very important in this equation. Proof. \[ egin{align*} 	ext{Var}[X] &= E[(X - \mu_X)^2] \ &= E \left[ X^2 ight] - E[2 X * \mu_X] + \mu_X^2 \ & = E \left[ X^2 ight] - 2 \mu_X * \mu_X + \mu_X^2 \ & = E \left[ X^2 ight] - \mu_X^2 \end{align*}\] Example 5.8 Returning again to Example 5.7 \[ egin{align*} E \left[ X^2 ight] &= \sum_{\mathcal{S}_X} x^2 \cdot f(x) \ &= (0^2)(0.10) + (1^2)(0.20) + \cdots + (4^2)(0.15) \ &= 6.05 \end{align*}\] We can now confirm our previous variance calculation: \[ \sigma^2_X = E \left[ X^2 ight] - \mu_X^2 = 6.05 - 2.15^2 = 1.4275 \] Similarly to Proposition 5.1, we can compute the variance of linear combinations. It is important to see in which ways this similar and, even more importantly, which ways is is different: Proposition 5.3 For the linear function \(h(X) = aX + b\), \[ 	ext{Var}[h(X)] = 	ext{Var}[aX + b] = a^2 	ext{Var}[X] \] In words, this means the variance of a linear function squares the multiplicative constant and eliminates the additive constant Proof. Using Proposition 5.1, \(E[aX + b] = a E[X] + b = a\mu_X + b\): \[ egin{align*} 	ext{Var}[aX + b] &= E[(aX + b - (a \mu_X + b))^2] \ & = E[(aX - a \mu_X)^2] \ & = E[a^2(X - \mu_X)^2] \ & = a^2E[(X - \mu_X)^2] \ & = a^2 	ext{Var}[X]\ \end{align*}\] Example 5.9 Returning to the context of Example 5.3, we have \[ E \left[ X^2 ight] = (0^2)(0.10) + (1^2)(0.15) + (2^2)(0.25) + (3^2)(0.30) + (4^2)(0.15) + (5^2)(0.05) = 7.5 \] and \(\sigma^2_X = E \left[ X^2 ight] - \mu_X^2 = 7.5 - 2.4^2 = 1.74\). Thus, \[ 	ext{Var}[h(X)] = 	ext{Var}[50X - 100] = 50^2 \sigma^2_X = (2500)(1.74) = 4350 \] 5.5 Means and Variances of Common Distributions 5.5.1 Binomial First, note that it is straightforward to derive the mean and variance of a Bernoulli rv. We have \[ E[X] = \mu_X = \sum_{\mathcal{S}_X} xf(x) = (0)(1-p) + (1)(p) = p \] and we will then use the shortcut formula to compute \(	ext{Var}(X)\). Since \(E \left[ X^2 ight] = p\), \[ 	ext{Var}[X] = \sigma^2_X = E \left[ X^2 ight] - \mu_X^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p) \] We can now obtain the mean and variance of a Binomial rv. Proposition 5.4 If \(Y \sim 	ext{Bin}(n, p)\), then \(E[Y] = np\) and \(	ext{Var}[Y] = np(1-p)\) Example 5.10 Recall the multiple choice exam referenced in Example 4.11. We defined the rv \(Y \sim 	ext{Bin}(n=20, p=0.25)\) to represent the number of correct answers out of the 20 multiple choice questions on the exam. What is the mean and standard deviation of the number of questions answered correctly? Solution: The mean is \(E[Y] = np = (20)(0.25) = 5\), and the standard deviation is \[ \sqrt{	ext{Var}[Y]} = \sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{(20)(0.25)(0.75)} = 1.936492 \] 5.5.2 Hypergeometric Proposition 5.5 With \(X \sim 	ext{Hypergeometric}(n, M, N)\), \[ E[X] = n  rac{M}{N}, \hspace{1cm} 	ext{Var}[X] = n  rac{M}{N}  rac{N-n}{N-1} \left( 1 -  rac{M}{N} ight) \] Example 5.11 Recall Example 4.13, where we defined the number of defective lightbulbs as \(X \sim 	ext{hypergeometric}(10, 8, 80)\). What are \(E[X]\) and \(	ext{Var}[X]\)? Solution: \(E[X] = 10 \left(  rac{8}{80} ight) = 1\) and \(	ext{Var}[X] = 10 \left(  rac{8}{80} ight) \left(  rac{80-10}{80-1} ight) \left( 1 -  rac{8}{80} ight) = 0.7974684\) We introduced the hypergeometric distribution as being related to the binomial distribution. A related note: let \(p\) denote \(M/N\) (the proportion of successes in the population), and note that we can now write the mean and variance of the hypergeometric distribution as follows: \[ E[X] = np, \hspace{1cm} 	ext{Var}[X] = \left(  rac{N-n}{N-1} ight) np(1-p) \] Comparing these results with those for the binomial distribution, we see that a finite population has no impact on the mean but requires a multiplicative adjustment to the variance. The factor \((N-n) / (N-1)\) is called the finite population correction factor. 5.5.3 Negative Binomial Proposition 5.6 With \(X \sim 	ext{NegBin}(r, p)\), \[ E[X] =  rac{r}{p}, \hspace{1cm} 	ext{Var}[X] = r  rac{1-p}{p^2} \] Example 5.12 As in Example 4.14, let the number of lightbulbs that will need to be inspected before we find the third defective bulb (\(X\)) be distributed as \(	ext{NegBin}(r=3, p=0.10)\). What are \(E[X]\) and \(	ext{Var}[X]\)? Solution: \(E[X] =  rac{3}{0.10} = 30\) and \(	ext{Var}[X] = 3 \left(  rac{1-0.10}{0.10^2} ight) = 270\). 5.5.4 Poisson Recall the limiting relationship between the binomial and Poisson distributions that we discussed in Section 4.4.2.4.1. That relationship can be used to reveal the mean and variance of a Poisson rv. In particular, the mean and variance of a \(	ext{Bin}(n, p)\) rv will approach those of a \(	ext{Poisson}(\lambda)\) rv. That is, \(np ightarrow \lambda\) and \(np(1-p) ightarrow \lambda\); the latter limit follows as a result of \(1-p\) approaching 1. Note that, for a Poisson rv, the mean equals the variance. These results can also be derived directly from the Poisson pmf and the definitions of mean and variance. Proposition 5.7 If \(X \sim 	ext{Poisson}(\lambda)\), then \(E[X] = 	ext{Var}[X] = \lambda\). Example 5.13 Recall Example 4.15, where we defined the number of emails received by a company's customer support service as \(X \sim 	ext{Poisson}(\lambda = 25)\). What are \(E[X]\) and \(	ext{Var}[X]\)? Solution: \(E[X] = 	ext{Var}[X] = 25\). 5.5.5 Exponential Proposition 5.8 With \(X \sim 	ext{Exp}(\lambda)\), \[ E[X] =  rac{1}{\lambda}, \quad 	ext{Var}[X] =  rac{1}{\lambda^2}. \] Example 5.14 Referencing Example 4.16, suppose that customers arrive at a coffee shop at an average rate of 5 per hour. The time \(X\) (in hours) until the next customer arrives follows an exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\lambda = 5\). What are \(E[X]\) and \(	ext{Var}[X]\)? Solution: \[ X \sim 	ext{Exp}(5). \] Using the formulas from the Proposition: \[ E[X] =  rac{1}{\lambda} =  rac{1}{5} = 0.2 \] \[ 	ext{Var}[X] =  rac{1}{\lambda^2} =  rac{1}{5^2} = 0.04 \] Thus, the expected waiting time between arrivals is 0.2 hours (or 12 minutes), and the variance quantifies the variability of waiting times. 5.5.6 Gamma Proposition 5.9 With \(X \sim 	ext{Gamma}(\alpha, \lambda)\), \[ E[X] =  rac{\alpha}{\lambda}, \quad 	ext{Var}[X] =  rac{\alpha}{\lambda^2} \] where: \(\alpha > 0\) is the shape parameter (the number of events), \(\lambda > 0\) is the rate parameter (events per unit time). Example 5.15 Referencing Example 4.18, suppose that the time (in minutes) a customer spends waiting in line at a bank follows a gamma distribution with parameters \(\alpha = 3\) (representing 3 phases in the service process) and \(\lambda = 0.5\) (events occurring at an average rate of 0.5 per minute). What are \(E[X]\) and \(	ext{Var}[X]\)? Solution: \[ X \sim 	ext{Gamma}(3, 0.5). \] Using the formulas from the Proposition: \[ E[X] =  rac{\alpha}{\lambda} =  rac{3}{0.5} = 6 \] \[ 	ext{Var}[X] =  rac{\alpha}{\lambda^2} =  rac{3}{0.5^2} = 12 \] 5.5.7 Chi-Squared Proposition 5.10 With \(X \sim \chi^2_{
u}\), \[ E[X] = 
u, \quad 	ext{Var}[X] = 2
u \] where \(
u\) represents the degrees of freedom. Example 5.16 Referencing Example 4.19, suppose a company monitors the sum of squared deviations in temperature readings from a machine. Based on historical data, the sum of squared deviations follows a chi-squared distribution with \(
u = 8\) degrees of freedom. What are \(E[X]\) and \(	ext{Var}[X]\)? Solution: \[ X \sim \chi^2_8 \] Using the formulas from the Proposition: \[ E[X] = 
u = 8, \quad 	ext{Var}[X] = 2
u = 16 \] Thus, the expected sum of squared deviations is 8, with variance 16. 5.6 Moment Generating Functions One way to characterize a random variable and its probability distribution is via its moments. The term moment here is used in exactly the same way as it is in physics whereby the zeroth moment is the total mass, the first moment corresponds to center of mass, and so on. Definition 5.6 The $k^{th} moment of a random variable \(X\) is \(E \left[ X^k ight]\). Notice that the mean \(\mu_X = E[X]\) is a moment (the "first" moment, since it corresponds to \(n=1\) in the definition). Similarly, the variance \(\sigma^2_X = E \left[ X^2 ight] - \mu_X^2\) involves the second moment \(E[X^2]\) (that is, \(k=2\)). There are other moments (e.g., skewness and kurtosis) that are of interest in some settings. Definition 5.7 The moment generating function (MGF) of \(X\) is \[ M_X(t) = E \left[ e^{tX} ight] \] This somewhat obscure looking function corresponds to the (inverse) Laplace transform, though this insight isn't important for how we will use the MGF. MGFs are useful as we can they can be used to find moments of random variable using the following result: Proposition 5.11 The \(k^{th}\) moment of \(X\) about the origin is given by the \(k^{th}\) derivative of \(M_X(t)\) evaluated at \(t=0\): \[ E \left[ X^k ight] =  rac{d^k}{dt^k} M_X(t) \Big|_{t=0} \] Example 5.17 The exponential distribution is commonly used in engineering applications to model time until failure for electronic components, mechanical systems, and communication networks. Let \(X \sim 	ext{Exp}(\lambda)\) have an exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\lambda > 0\). The MGF of \(X\) is: \[ M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = \int_0^\infty e^{tx} \lambda e^{-\lambda x} dx. \] Solving the integral gives: \[ M_X(t) =  rac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \quad t < \lambda. \] To find the expected value of \(X\), we differentiate once: \[ E[X] = M'_X(0) =  rac{1}{\lambda}. \] To find the variance, we differentiate twice: \[ E \left[ X^2 ight] = M''_X(0) =  rac{2}{\lambda^2}, \] \[ 	ext{Var}[X] = E \left[ X^2 ight] - \left( E[X] ight)^2 =  rac{2}{\lambda^2} - \left( rac{1}{\lambda}ight)^2 =  rac{1}{\lambda^2}. \] Thus, we recover the known results: \[ E[X] =  rac{1}{\lambda}, \quad 	ext{Var}[X] =  rac{1}{\lambda^2}. \] In reliability engineering, this result tells us that if a machine part has an average lifespan of 500 hours, then the failure rate is \(\lambda = 1/500\), and the variance quantifies the variability in failure times.

Chapter 6 The Normal Distribution The Normal distribution is one of the most fundamental and widely used probability distributions in Statistics. First studied in the 18th century by Abraham de Moivre and later formalized by Carl Friedrich Gauss (leading to its alternative name the Gaussian distribution), the Normal distribution arose from investigations into errors in astronomical measurements. Gauss’ work in the early 19th century demonstrated that random errors in repeated observations tended to follow the same bell-shaped curve. Since then, the Normal distribution has become a cornerstone of probability and statistics, describing a vast array of real-world phenomena. It models natural variations in biological traits (e.g., human heights, blood pressure, IQ scores), economic and financial data (e.g., stock returns, measurement errors in production processes), and even physical and engineering systems (e.g., noise in electronic signals, material tolerances in manufacturing). More so, the central role of the Normal distribution is due to the Central Limit Theorem, which explains why sums (and hence averages and proportions) of large numbers of independent random variables have an approximately Normal distribution; we will cover this topic in detail in Chapter 8. Because of its mathematical properties and real-world relevance, the Normal distribution serves as the foundation for many statistical methods, including confidence intervals (Chapter 9), hypothesis tests (Chapter 10), and regression analysis (Chapters 13 and 14). 6.1 The Normal and Standard Normal Distributions 6.1.1 The Normal Distribution Definition 6.1 A continuous rv \(X\) has a Normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2 > 0\), written \(X \sim N([\mu, \sigma^2]{#def-the-normal-distribution-probabilities-of-n-mu-sigma-2})\), has pdf: \[ f(x) =  rac{1}{ \sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{- rac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}, \quad -\infty < x < \infty \] The Normal distribution has a characteristic symmetric bell shape, with most of the probability mass concentrated near the mean \(\mu\). The spread of the distribution is determined by \(\sigma\), which is the square root of the variance (\(\sigma = +\sqrt{\sigma^2}\)); larger values of \(\sigma\) correspond to wider, more spread-out distributions, while smaller values of \(\sigma\) correspond to narrower, more concentrated distributions. Figure 6.1 shows the pdfs of three example Normal distributions. Figure 6.1: Example Normal distribution pdfs with different means and standard deviations 6.1.2 The Standard Normal Distribution A special case of the Normal distribution, known as the standard Normal distribution, corresponds to when \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Definition 6.2 A continuous rv \(Z\) has a standard Normal distribution, written \(Z \sim N(0,1)\), has pdf \[ f(z) =  rac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, \quad -\infty < z < \infty \] As the standard Normal distribution has \(\mu = 0\), the pdf is centered at 0. In this textbook, \(Z\) will always be used to represent the standard normal. 6.2 Standardization The pdf of the Normal distribution is impossible to integrate analytically in general. Historically, before the widespread use of computers, scientists relied on standardized probability tables. Using standardization, any Normal random variable can be transformed into a standard normal (and vice versa). Hence, probability calculations could be performed using a single table rather than computing values separately for each possible mean and variance. While modern computing has made it easy to work directly with any Normal distribution, standardization is at the core of many methods, such as Hypothesis testing @ref(hypothesis_testing). Definition 6.3 The process of going from a Normal random variable to a standard Normal random variable is called standardization. In particular, if \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then \[ Z =  rac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0,1) \] Similarly, by inverting this transformation, we can unstandardize a standard Normal: \[ X = \mu + \sigma Z \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2) \] (note the use of the standard deviation \(\sigma\) in these formulae; hence the consistent usage of the word 'standard'). The simplicity of this result belies its utility. As a first application, let's define and explore a famous term: \(z\)-score. 6.3 \(z\)-scores Standardization is a process that allows us to compare values from different distributions by expressing them on a common scale. A \(z\)-score represents how many standard deviations an observed value is from the mean of its distribution. This idea is especially useful when we want to assess which of two values is more unusual or extreme, even if they come from populations with different means and standard deviations. A \(z\)-score will always look like \(z =  rac{	extrm{value} - 	extrm{mean}}{	extrm{sd}}\). Example 6.1 Suppose biologists are monitoring the size of largemouth bass in two different lakes. Let \(X\) represent the weight (in grams) of a randomly caught bass. The weight distribution depends on which lake is being sampled: In Lake Bryan, \(X \sim N(1200, 300^2)\) In Somerville Lake, \(Y \sim N(1000, 200^2)\) Now suppose that a 1700g bass is caught in Lake Bryan, and a 1500g bass is caught in Somerville Lake. Which fish is more "unusual" or "extreme" relative to its lake's population if bass? To find these values is more extreme, we can compute z-scores: Lake Bryan: \(z =  rac{1700 - 1200}{300} = 1.67\) Somerville Lake: \(z =  rac{1500 - 1000}{200} = 2.50\) Although the 1700g fish is heavier in absolute terms, the 1500g fish from Somerville Lake is more extreme relative to the distribution in that lake. One way to think about the above \(z\)-scores is as follows: the 1700g fish from Lake Bryan is 1.67 standard deviations away from the Lake Bryan population mean, while the 1500g fish from Somerville Lake is 2.5 standard deviations away from the Somerville Lake population mean. Figure 6.2 shows the two distributions and the observed values. Figure 6.2: Comparison of observed fish weights relative to their respective distributions 6.4 Probabilities 6.4.1 Computing Standard Normal Probabilities First, we will explore calculating probabilites from the standard normal distribution. This will be an important topic for computing p-values (Chapter 10), among other applications. Example 6.2 Figure 6.3 shows the pdf of the standard Normal distribution. In the figure, the probability \(P(Z \leq z)\) is shown by shading the area under the standard Normal pdf to the left of \(z\) for \(z = 1.6449\). In particular, \(P(Z \leq 1.6449) = 0.95\). Notice that, as the probabilities must sum to one, \(P(Z > z) = 1 - P(Z \leq z)\). Referencing the figure again, since the area under the pdf to the left of 1.6449 is 0.95, we have that the area under the pdf to the right of 1.6449 is 0.05. We can verify the above calculations in R using the pnorm function (think of p as meaning probability). pnorm(1.6449) ## [1] 0.9500048 1 - pnorm(1.6449) ## [1] 0.04999522 Figure 6.3: Standard Normal pdf and a cumulative probability In addition to left-tail (cumulative) and right-tail probabilities, we can integrate the pdf to obtain a probability corresponding to rv values between two values. For example, consider the probability \(P(-0.6745 \leq Z \leq 1.6449)\). Figure 6.4 shows this probability as the shaded area under the standard Normal pdf between \(-0.6745\) and \(1.6449\), which happens to equal \(\approx 0.70\). We saw in Section 4.3 that a probability for an interval of values can be written as a difference of cdf probabilities. In our example, we have that \[ P(-0.6745 \leq Z \leq 1.6449) = P(Z \leq 1.6449) - P(Z \leq -0.6745) \] pnorm(1.6449) - pnorm(-0.6745) ## [1] 0.700008 Figure 6.4: Standard Normal pdf and the probability for an interval of values Returning to the \(z\)-score example (Example 6.1), we can find the probability of having caught the particular fish from each lake. The observed \(z\)-scores are 1.67 from Lake Bryan and 2.5 from Somerville Lake, indicating the largemouth bass from Somerville Lake was more unusual. Another, related way of describing this would be via probability: a low probability indicates an observation is more unusual as well: For the 1700g fish from Lake Bryan with \(z\)-score 1.67: \[ P(Z \leq 1.67) \] For the 1500g fish from Somerville Lake with \(z\)-score 2.50: \[ P(Z \leq 2.50) \] These probabilities can be once again computed using the pnorm function in R: pnorm(1.67) # in Lake Bryan ## [1] 0.9525403 pnorm(2.50) # in Somerville Lake ## [1] 0.9937903 Thus, the 1700g fish is just above the 95th percentile for Lake Bryan, while the 1500g fish is just above the 99th percentile for Somerville Lake. 6.4.2 Computing Normal Probabilities We can actually compute the above probabilities directly by using the pnorm function in R more generally. In example 6.1, we considered In Lake Bryan, \(X \sim N(1200, 300^2)\) In Somerville Lake, \(Y \sim N(1000, 200^2)\) If we were only interested in the probability of getting bass that weighed 1700g and 1500g, respectively, we could calculate it directly: pnorm(1700, 1200, 300) # in Lake Bryan ## [1] 0.9522096 pnorm(1500, 1000, 200) # in Somerville Lake ## [1] 0.9937903 hence, \[ P(X \leq 1700) = 0.9522 \] and \[ P(Y \leq 1500) = 0.9938 \] The fact that these answers match the ones using the standard Normal is no coincidence; finding the \(z\)-score and using the standard Normal or using the (general) Normal directly will always result in the same solution. Warning The pnorm function uses the standard deviation \(\sigma\), not the variance \(\sigma^2\)! To demonstrate this point, let's do another example. Example 6.3 Suppose a factory produces cylindrical rods whose diameters (in millimeters) are Normally distributed with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 2. Let \(X\) represent the diameter of a randomly selected rod: \(X \sim N(50, 2^2)\). The manufacturing specifications require rods to be between 48 mm and 54 mm in diameter. What is the probability that a randomly selected rod meets this specification? Solution: We can compute this probability directly in R using the pnorm function: pnorm(54, mean = 50, sd = 2) - pnorm(48, mean = 50, sd = 2) ## [1] 0.8185946 Alternatively, we can standardize both bounds and compute the equivalent probability under the standard Normal distribution: \[ P(48 \leq X \leq 54) = P\left(  rac{48 - 50}{2} \leq  rac{X - 50}{2} \leq  rac{54 - 50}{2} ight) = P(-1 \leq Z \leq 2) \] pnorm(2) - pnorm(-1) ## [1] 0.8185946 As expected, both calculations yield the same result. Figure 6.5 shows the relationship between the original distribution and its standardized version. The shaded areas represent the same probability under each distribution. Figure 6.5: Probability for an interval in an arbitrary Normal distribution alongside corresponding probability in the standard Normal distribution In the preceding example, our desired calculation boiled down to the probability that our rv, following an arbitrary Normal distribution, would fall between the mean minus one standard deviation and the mean plus two standard deviations. There is a relevant rule of thumb that can be applied to approximate such a probability based on a Normal distribution. Note: For a Normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), the following approximate probabilities hold: \(P(\mu - \sigma \leq X \leq \mu + \sigma) \approx 0.68\) \(P(\mu - 2\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 2\sigma) \approx 0.95\) \(P(\mu - 3\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 3\sigma) \approx 0.997\) These are sometimes referred to as the Empirical Rule or the 68–95–99.7 Rule, and they provide a useful reference for assessing how typical or unusual an observation is under a Normal distribution. In Example 6.3, our desired probability could be written as \(P(\mu - \sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 2\sigma)\), where \(X \sim N(50, 2^2)\), or equivalently \(P(-1 \leq Z \leq 2)\), where \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\). Note that we can write \[ P(-1 \leq Z \leq 2) = P(-1 \leq Z \leq 0) + P(0 \leq Z \leq 2) \] According to the Empirical Rule, because the Normal distribution is symmetric about the mean, we have \(P(-1 \leq Z \leq 0) \approx 0.68 / 2 = 0.34\) and \(P(0 \leq Z \leq 2) \approx 0.95 / 2 = 0.475\). Thus, we have the approximation \[ P(48 \leq X \leq 54) = P(-1 \leq Z \leq 2) \approx 0.34 + 0.475 = 0.815 \] 6.5 Quantiles In Section 2.5.2, we introduced the idea of a sample quartile. As with most sample statistics, there is a corresponding population parameter. The most general term used in this context is quantile. Think of this as a generalization of quartile or percentile. In particular, the \(p\)th population quantile is the value such that the probability of being less than that value is \(p\). In what follows, we discuss quantiles of the standard Normal distribution (from section 6.1.1). In section 6.5.2 we will show how to compute general Normal quantiles, both from converting the standard Normal quantiles then by computing the quantiles directly. 6.5.1 Computing Standard Normal Quantiles A convention that we will make use of later in the book (e.g., Chapters 9 and 10 on confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, respectively) is to use the symbol \(z_{\alpha}\) to represent the number in the standard Normal distribution such that \(P(Z > z_{\alpha}) = \alpha\). Note that, because \(P(Z > z_{\alpha}) = \alpha\), we have that \(P(Z \leq z_{\alpha}) = 1-\alpha\). In other words, \(z_{\alpha}\) is simply the \((1-\alpha)	imes 100\)th quantile of the standard Normal distribution. \[ z_p = -z_{1 - p} \] We can use the R function qnorm to obtain quantiles (and hence \(z_{\alpha}\) values) for the standard Normal distribution. qnorm(0.95) ## [1] 1.644854 qnorm(0.05) ## [1] -1.644854 Note that other named distributions have analogous functions in R; see e.g. pbinom & qbinom for the binomial distribution, pexp & qexp for the exponential distribution, etc. Note also that we will mimic the \(z_{\alpha}\) notation with other probability distributions. For example, $^2_{; \(n - 1\)}$ would indicate the \((1 - \alpha) 	imes 100\)th quantile of the \(\chi^2\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom. 6.5.2 Computing Normal Quantiles The following Proposition states a relationship between a quantile of an arbitrary Normal distribution and the analogous quantile of the standard Normal distribution. Proposition 6.1 Let \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) be a Normally distributed random variable, and let \(z_p\) denote the \(p\)th quantile of the standard Normal distribution (i.e., \(P(Z \leq z_p) = p\) for \(Z \sim N(0,1)\)). Then, the \(p\)th quantile of \(X\) is given by: \[ x_p = \mu + z_p \cdot \sigma \] That is, to obtain a quantile of an arbitrary Normal distribution, we can scale and shift the corresponding standard Normal quantile. Example 6.4 Suppose systolic blood pressure in a particular population of adult women follows a Normal distribution with mean \(\mu = 120\) mmHg and standard deviation \(\sigma = 15\) mmHg (that is, \(X \sim N(120, 15^2)\)). What is the 95th percentile of systolic blood pressure in this population? Solution: We can answer this question in two ways: Use qnorm directly: qnorm(0.95, mean = 120, sd = 15) ## [1] 144.6728 The 95th percentile of systolic blood pressure is 144.6728 mmHg. Use the standard Normal quantile and apply the Proposition: qnorm(0.95) ## [1] 1.644854 The 95th quantile of the standard Normal distribution is about 1.6449. Applying the formula from the Proposition gives \[ x_{0.95} = 120 + 1.6449 \cdot 15 = 144.6735 \] with the difference relative to the earlier result being due to rounding. Figure 6.6 shows the Normal pdf with the 95th quantile marked and the area under the curve to the left of it shaded in. Figure 6.6: Normal distribution of systolic blood pressure with 95th percentile shown 6.6 Q-Q Plots for Checking Normality One of the most commonly used graphical tools for assessing whether a dataset plausibly comes from a Normal distribution is the quantile-quantile plot, or Q-Q plot. A Q-Q plot compares the quantiles of the observed data to the corresponding quantiles of a theoretical distribution—in this case, the Normal distribution. If the data follow a Normal distribution, then the points on the Q-Q plot will approximately fall along a straight line. Systematic deviations from linearity suggest departures from Normality. Interpretation: Points that fall roughly along the line indicate approximate Normality. A curved pattern suggests skewness: Points that curve upward suggest right-skewness (long right tail). Points that curve downward suggest left-skewness (long left tail). Heavy-tailed or light-tailed distributions may show as deviations at the ends of the plot. Below, we simulate three datasets and construct a panel of plots that includes a histogram and a Q-Q plot for each dataset: 1. Normal distribution 2. Right-skewed distribution (exponential) 3. Left-skewed distribution (negative exponential) set.seed(42) # Sample size n <- 100 # Simulated data normal_data <- rnorm(n) right_skewed <- rexp(n, rate = 1) left_skewed <- -rexp(n, rate = 1) # Plot settings par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) # Normal hist(normal_data, main = "Histogram: Normal", xlab = "", col = "lightgray") qqnorm(normal_data, main = "Q-Q Plot: Normal") qqline(normal_data, col = "blue", lwd = 2) # Right-skewed hist(right_skewed, main = "Histogram: Right-Skewed", xlab = "", col = "lightgray") qqnorm(right_skewed, main = "Q-Q Plot: Right-Skewed") qqline(right_skewed, col = "blue", lwd = 2) # Left-skewed hist(left_skewed, main = "Histogram: Left-Skewed", xlab = "", col = "lightgray") qqnorm(left_skewed, main = "Q-Q Plot: Left-Skewed") qqline(left_skewed, col = "blue", lwd = 2) Figure 6.7: Histograms and Q-Q plots for three datasets: Normal (top), right-skewed (middle), and left-skewed (bottom) These plots illustrate how Q-Q plots reveal distributional shape: The Q-Q plot for the Normal data shows points that mostly fall along a straight line. The right-skewed data deviate upward in the tails. The left-skewed data deviate downward in the tails. Q-Q plots are a valuable visual diagnostic, especially when interpreted in conjunction with histograms and contextual knowledge of the data. For large datasets, even minor departures from Normality may appear in a Q-Q plot, while for small datasets, random variation may obscure real patterns. 6.7 t Distribution The t distribution arises frequently in statistical inference, particularly when conducting inference on a population mean based on a small sample. It is similar in shape to the standard Normal distribution but has heavier tails, which reflect the additional uncertainty associated with estimating the population standard deviation from the sample. Definition 6.4 Let \(Z\) be a standard Normal random variable and let \(V\) be an independent chi-squared random variable with \(
u\) degrees of freedom. Then the random variable \[ T =  rac{Z}{\sqrt{V / 
u}} \] follows a t distribution with \(
u\) degrees of freedom, denoted \(T \sim t_
u\). The t distribution is symmetric about 0 and becomes increasingly similar to the standard Normal distribution as the degrees of freedom increase. Figure 6.8 shows a few t distributions for various values of \(
u\). Figure 6.8: Example t distribution pdfs compared to the standard Normal pdf As with other common named probability distributions, you can generate random numbers, compute probabilities, obtain quantiles, etc. for a t distribution with the R functions rt, pt, qt, and dt. Our first usage of the t distribution will be in Chapter 9. In particular, we will make use of the notation \(t_{\alpha,n-1}\) to be the analogous object to \(z_{\alpha}\) as we defined in Section 6.5.1: n <- 30 nu <- n-1 alpha <- .01 t_alpha <- qt(1-alpha,nu) t_alpha ## [1] 2.462021 This means that the degrees of freedom is \(
u = n-1 = 29\) and hence \(t_{.01,29} =\) 2.4620214.
