This is the inverse of the CDF. qqnorm() Syntax: qqnorm(y, main = "title") This function returns a Q-Q Plot (Quantile-Quantile Plot). This is a graphical tool for checking if the supplied data vector y follows a normal distribution. If the data points lie close to a straight line, then the data are approximately normal. An optional title can be given to this plot with the argument main qqline() Syntax: qqline(y, col = "color", lwd = 2) After calling the qqnorm() function, the qqline() function will add a visual guiding line that will help determine if the data follow a straight line. If the points lie close to a straight line, the data are approximately normal. Deviations indicate some non-normality (e.g., skewness, heavy tails). We can change the color and width of the line with the optional arguments col and lwd. 20.7 Joint and Conditional Distributions 20.7.1 Definitions Covariance: The covariance of \(X\) and \(Y\) is defined via: \(\operatorname{Cov}[X,Y] = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]\). This is a sub case of the expected value of a general function where we take \(h(X, Y) = \left( X - E[X] ight) \left( Y - E[Y] ight)\). Remember that \(E[X]\) and \(E[Y]\) are constants. For discrete and continuous random variables, we take the double sum or double integral. Discrete: \(\sum_x \sum_y (x - E[X])(y - E[Y]) f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) Continuous: \(\iint (x - E[X])(y - E[Y]) f_{X,Y}(x, y) dx \, dy\) However, it's often easier to calculate \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]\, E[Y]\) Correlation: The correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\) is given by: \(\operatorname{Cor}[X,Y] =  rac{\operatorname{Cov}[X,Y]}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y}\) where \(\sigma_X = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}, 	ext{ and } \sigma_Y = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}\) are calculated as usual. Joint PMF: For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the joint PMF is \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X = x 	ext{ and } Y = y)\). It satisfies: \(\sum_x \sum_y f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1\) and \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0\). We often define the joint pmf point-wise using a table (but not always). Marginal PMF: The marginal PMF of \(X\) is obtained by summing out \(Y\): $ f_X(x) = y f{X,Y}(x,y) $ Similarly for \(Y\): $ f_Y(y) = x f{X,Y}(x,y) $ Joint PDF: For continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the joint PDF \(f_{X,Y}(x, y)\) is the function that satisfies: \(P((X, Y) \in A) = \iint_A f_{X,Y}(x, y)\, dx \, dy\) Marginal PDF: The marginal PDF of \(X\) is: \(f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y) dy\) Similarly for \(Y\): $f_Y(y) = {-}^{} f{X,Y}(x, y) dx $ Conditional probability function: \(f_{Y|X}(y | x) =  rac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)} \quad 	ext{if } f_X(x) > 0\) Conditional Expected Value: The conditional expectated value works the same as the regular expectation, except we swap the pmf/pdf with the conditional pmf/pdf (fixed at a particular point \(x\)) Discrete: \(E[Y | X = x] = \sum_y y \cdot f_{Y|X}(y | x)\) Continuous: \(E[Y | X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y \cdot f_{Y|X}(y | x) dy\) Expected Value of a General Function: Like in the previous chapter with expectation, we can take the expected value of a general function \(h(X, Y)\) over jointly distributed random variables. Discrete: \(E[h(X,Y)] = \sum_x \sum_y h(x, y) \cdot f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) Continuous: \(E[h(X,Y)] = \iint h(x, y) \cdot f_{X,Y}(x, y) dx \, dy\) It's worth noting that the functions \(h(X, Y) = X\), \(h(X, Y) = Y\), and \(h(X,Y) = XY\) are valid for this rule. Independent Random Variables: \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent whenever: \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y)\) for all \(x, y\). Mutually Independent Random Variables: Random variables \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) are mutually independent if every subset is independent. Intuitively, this means that we are able to pick any collection of the \(X\)'s out of \(X_1,\ldots X_n\) and maintain independence. Important facts about Covariance and Correlation: If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then \(\operatorname{Cov}[X,Y] = 0\) and \(\operatorname{Cor}[X,Y] = 0\) If \(X\) and \(Y\) have \(\operatorname{Cov}[X,Y] = 0\) or \(\operatorname{Cor}[X,Y] = 0\) that does not mean they're independent. Linear transformations of \(X\) and \(Y\) have the covariance formula: \(\operatorname{Cov}[aX + b, cY + d] = ac \cdot \operatorname{Cov}[X,Y]\) Linear transformations of \(X\) and \(Y\) have the correlation formula: \(\operatorname{Cor}[aX + b, cY + d] = \operatorname{Cor}[X,Y]\) Correlation is always between \(-1\) and \(1\): \(|\operatorname{Cor}[X,Y]| \leq 1\) 20.8 Sampling Distributions and Central Limit Theorem 20.8.1 Definitions Central Limit Theorem (CLT): Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) be i.i.d. random variables with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\). As \(n 	o \infty\), the distribution of the sample mean ${X approaches a normal distribution: \( ar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left( \mu,  rac{\sigma^2}{n} ight)\) This holds for (nearly) any choice of distribution generating \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\). The CLT justifies using normal-based inference for large samples. Sampling Distribution: The sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic when viewed as a random variable. In other words, it describes how the statistic would vary across many repeated samples of the same size from the same population. Statistic: A statistic is any function of a sample of data. That is, any quantity computed using only the sample values \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) is a statistic. Some examples of a statistics include the sample mean, the sample median, or the sample standard deviation. Random Sample: A collection of random variables \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) is called a random sample of size \(n\) from a population if each \(X_i\) has the same probability distribution and each \(X_i\) are independent random variables. If this is so, we say that \(X_i\) are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d) random variables. Sample Mean \( ar{X}\): The sample mean is simply the average of the sample \(X_1,\ldots, X_n\) \( ar{X} =  rac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^n X_i =  rac{X_1 + \cdots + X_n}{n}\) Standard Error: The standard error of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution and is written \(	ext{SE}\). Sample Standard Deviation \(S\): This is the sample standard deviation. It has formula \(S_X = \sqrt{ rac{1}{n - 1}\sum_{i = 1}^n (X_i -  ar{X})^2}\) Expectation and Variance of Linear Combination: For a linear combination of independent random variables: \(Y = a_1 X_1 + a_2 X_2 + \dots + a_n X_n\) We have: \(E[Y] = a_1 E[X_1] + a_2 E[X_2] + \dots + a_n E[X_n]\) \(	ext{Var}(Y) = a_1^2 	ext{Var}(X_1) + a_2^2 	ext{Var}(X_2) + \dots + a_n^2 	ext{Var}(X_n)\) Expectation and Variance of Sample Mean: Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) be a random sample from some distribution. Write \(E[X_i] = \mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2\). Take \( ar{X} =  rac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\), we have: \(E[ ar{X}] = \mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}( ar{X}) =  rac{\sigma^2}{n}\) This follows immediately from the expectation and variance of a linear combination after taking all \(a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_n =  rac{1}{n}\). This property holds for any choice of distribution. Distribution of Sample Mean from Normal Distribution: If \(X_1, \ldots X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) (i.i.d) then: \( ar{X} \sim N\left(\mu,  rac{\sigma^2}{n} ight)\) That is, if \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) are normally distributed, then \( ar{X}\) is also normally distributed (with a smaller variance). This is a special property of the normal distribution. It works for any sample size \(n\), even the smallest sample sizes like \(n = 1\), \(n = 2\), or \(n = 3\). The sample proportion (\(\hat{p}\)):It has formula \(\hat{p} =  rac{	ext{# Successes}}{n}\) It is used whenever our data is binary, meaning that there are two possible outcomes, a "success" or a "failure". A "success" has different meanings depending on the study, it is not necessarily a "good" or "bad" outcome. 20.8.2 R Commands matrix() Syntax: matrix(data, nrow, ncol, byrow) This function will turn data (numeric) into a matrix of nrow many rows and ncol many columns. Confidence Intervals are calculated using an observed value of a sample statistic, a pivot, and a quantile of that pivot's sampling distribution. Pivot: A special type of statistic that combine both the data and the parameter of interest in such a way that allow for the sampling distribution to be completely known. We use pivots to construct confidence intervals. Precision: The width of our confidence interval represents the precision in our estimate of the population parameter. A narrower interval means that we have a more precise interval. A related question we may ask is to find a necessary sample size \(n\) so that the width of the confidence interval is no more than \(w\) wide in the "population mean and \(\sigma^2\) known" case. \(n = \left (  rac{2\cdot z_{\alpha/2}\cdot \sigma}{w}ight)^2\) Bootstrap Intervals (Percentile Method): This is a procedure that approximates the sampling distributions and confidence intervals of complex/non-standard statistics. It is a powerful and relatively easy to implement procedure that works in a wide variety of contexts. However, it has several known limitations which can be partially addressed by more advanced bootstrap methods. Interpretation of a Confidence Interval: If we were to repeat the study many times and compute a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval each time, then \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) percent of those constructed confidence intervals would contain the true parameter value. Crucially: each individual constructed interval either contains the parameter or it doesn't, no probability about it! Quantiles of a Normal Distribution: The quantile \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the number such that \(P(Z \leq z_{\alpha/2}) = 1 -  rac{\alpha}{2}\) for \(Z \sim N(0,1)\). Or equivalently, \(P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) =  rac{\alpha}{2}\). Consequently, \(P(- z_{\alpha/2} \leq Z \leq z_{\alpha/2}) = 1 - \alpha\) for \(Z\sim N(0,1)\). If the data provide strong enough evidence, we may reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_A\). The alternative hypothesis will have one of 3 signs in its statement: \(
eq,\, >,\, <\). The alternative hypothesis will have the opposite sign of the null hypothesis. Test Statistic: Test Statistic is a numerical summary calculated using the sample data. It is used to evaluate if our data is consistent with the null hypothesis. A test statistic often have a null distribution, which is the sampling distribution of the test statistic given that the null hypothesis is true. For the typical hypothesis tests, the null distribution can either be the Standard Normal \(N(0,1)\), a t-distribution, or a \(\chi^2\)-distribution (with some \(
u\)-degrees of freedom). p-value: The p-value represents the probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme or more under the null hypothesis. Remember: If the p-value is low, reject the null. Otherwise, we do not reject the null hypothesis. Type I Error (type 1 error): occurs whenever we reject the null hypothesis even though it is is true. Type II error (type 2 error): occurs whenever we fail to reject the null hypothesis even though it is false. Remember: we always assume the null hypothesis is true and either reject it or fail to reject it, based on supplied evidence. Power: Power is the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative hypothesis is true. Mathematically, \(	ext{Power} = 1 - P(	ext{Type II error})\). Power depends on several factors, some of which can be out of our control in a study. In general, we want our hypothesis test to have high power. Significance Level (\(\alpha\)): The significance level is a value set before conducting a hypothesis test. Mathematically, the significance level is the probability of a Type I error. Rejection Region: The rejection region is a set of values for the test statistic that would result in a rejection of the null hypothesis. We can think of these as the "extreme-outcomes" that should be unlikely under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. Null Hypothesis \(\left( H_0ight)\): The null hypothesis is a skeptical or status-quo statement about the population parameter. When we are performing a hypothesis test, we assume that the null hypothesis is true and test (with a test statistic) whether the observed data provide enough evidence to reject it. The null hypothesis will have one of 3 signs in its statement: \(=,\, \leq,\, \geq\). It will always have an "equal" somewhere in the sign. Logical Steps in a Hypothesis Test: Formulate the null hypothesis \(H_0\) and the alternative hypothesis \(H_A\) and significance level \(\alpha\). Assume the null hypothesis is true unless we're presented with evidence that strongly suggests otherwise. Before gathering any data, choose a test statistic \(T\) and figure out its null distribution. Run the experiment and compute the observed value of the test statistic \(T_{obs}\). Compute the p-value, which is the probability of observing a test statistic \(T\) as extreme or more extreme than the observed test statistic \(T_{obs}\).
